analysis.one_liner: Bans colleges from forcing students into arbitration or blocking class-action lawsuits.
analysis.headline: The bill died in the Senate committee it was sent to on the day it was introduced; it never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would do two things. It would take away colleges' ability to make students sign away their day in court as a condition of enrolling, and it would bar any college that takes federal student aid from enforcing restrictions — like forced arbitration, class-action bans, or chosen venues — on a student's right to sue it in court. The bill never moved after being sent to the Senate's education committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Students at colleges that participate in federal student aid programs. Under the bill they could sue their school in court, join class actions, keep a jury trial, and would no longer be bound by fine-print arbitration clauses in enrollment agreements.
analysis.who_benefits_short: College students with claims against schools

how_it_helps.text: The bill removes arbitration agreements in student enrollment contracts from the federal law that otherwise compels courts to enforce them, so a student's enrollment contract could not take the courtroom option away [S2] [S3].

It adds a condition to the Higher Education Act: any college in federal student aid programs, including work-study, cannot require or enforce any restriction on a student's ability to bring a claim in court, individually or with others, including limits on jury trials, choice of law, or venue [S2] [S3].

Because colleges could no longer block group lawsuits, students with similar, small-dollar claims — the common pattern when a school's recruiting or lending practices harm many students at once — could pool their cases instead of being pushed into one-by-one private arbitration [S2] [S3].
The bill takes effect one year after enactment, giving schools time to revise enrollment paperwork [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Colleges and universities — especially schools that use enrollment arbitration clauses to avoid group lawsuits over recruiting, loan, or refund practices — would face court claims they currently shield themselves from, with litigation and settlement costs that could be passed into tuition or absorbed by school budgets.

drawbacks.text: Schools and arbitration's defenders argue that individual arbitration is faster and cheaper for a single student than district-court litigation, so removing it could mean some small claims simply go unfiled [S3] — this is the standard industry objection; the bill's premise is that what students lose in private speed they gain in public accountability and group leverage [S2].
Colleges would bear new litigation and settlement exposure, and any added defense costs could ultimately show up in tuition or fees rather than school endowments [S3].

The bill only covers enrollment agreements with institutions of higher education, so disputes with third-party contractors a school hires, or non-degree programs outside the Higher Education Act definition, would not be affected [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is straightforward: students give up the (arguably overrated) convenience of private arbitration and gain back the courtroom, jury trials, and class actions; colleges lose a shield from group litigation. For students, the gain is real but only matters when a school actually injures them. The costs to schools are real but indirect, and the bill's narrow scope means third-party disputes stay in arbitration. It is a modestly drawn bill, but it died without ever being examined in committee.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee the same day, and nothing further ever happened to it before Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Richard Durbin introduced the bill on March 7, 2017, joined by eight Democratic cosponsors [S1] [S4].
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions [S5].
The action record shows no hearing, no committee vote, no floor action of any kind after that referral; the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019 with the bill still sitting in committee [S5] [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Colleges — particularly those that use enrollment contracts to steer disputes into private arbitration and block group lawsuits — kept that shield without ever having to defend it in a hearing or a vote. Arbitration providers kept the education-institution segment of their market.

for.name: Sen. Richard Durbin
for.role: U.S. Senator from Illinois; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill in the Senate and led it through referral.

against.name: Senate HELP Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Sen. Lamar Alexander (R-TN)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on the day of introduction and took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no committee vote — for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all eight cosponsors were Democrats; the Republican-run committee that received the bill never acted on it, and no Republican supported it.

industries.industry: Colleges and universities, especially for-profit schools
industries.note: The bill would strip schools' ability to force students into arbitration and block class actions, exposing them to court suits over practices like aggressive recruiting or student-lending disputes. Their interest in keeping that shield runs directly against students' ability to hold them accountable.

industries.industry: Arbitration providers and the consumer-arbitration industry
industries.note: Colleges' enrollment contracts are a source of private-arbitration business; the bill removes the legal compulsion that enforces those clauses, shrinking the market these firms serve. Their gain from the status quo is students' loss of a courtroom.

With class actions and jury trials restored for student claims, plaintiff-side litigation work against colleges would expand. This only pays off where students have real claims, so it runs alongside students' interests.
